segments.english: He sent out the raven, and it went back and forth until the waters had dried from off the earth.
segments.literal: and-sent [object-marker]-the-raven and-went going-out and-returning until drying-of the-waters from-upon the-earth

tokens.note: infinitive absolute: continuous action, 'kept going out'
infinitive construct, 'until the drying of the waters'

phrases.english: and it went back and forth
phrases.literal: 'and-went going-out and-returning': two infinitive absolutes after a finite verb express repeated or continuing motion

grammar: וַיֵּצֵא יָצוֹא וָשׁוֹב: a finite verb followed by two infinitive absolutes; the pair gives continued, repeated motion.
The etnaḥta on הָעֹרֵב ends the first clause; the zaqef qaton on וָשׁוֹב sets off 'went out and back' from the time clause.
עַד יְבֹשֶׁת הַמַּיִם: עַד with an infinitive construct (feminine form of יבשׁ) forms a time clause.
מֵעַל is a compound preposition, 'from upon', so 'from off'.
segments.note: The Hebrew does not say whether the raven landed anywhere, nor whether it came back to the ark; the English keeps that openness with 'back and forth'. The pack lemma for the infinitive absolutes is יצא and שׁוב; the data are kept.

commentary.summary: Rashi reads יָצוֹא וָשׁוֹב as the raven going and circling round the ark and not going on its errand, because it suspected Noah about its mate (Sanhedrin 108b). The English 'back and forth' fits this but does not say it.

Rashi: 'its plain sense is as it sounds' (the raven went and came until the waters dried); the Aggadic reading that the raven was kept for a later errand in Elijah's drought (1 Kings 17) is homily and does not bear on the English.
Onkelos has the raven 'going out and returning' until the waters dried from the earth.
Radak: the raven would eat carrion and bring back flesh if the waters were low; Noah saw it go in and out of its nest until the waters dried.

apparatus: Rashi and Radak differ on where the raven went; the Hebrew gives no destination.

segments.english: Then he sent out the dove from him, to see whether the waters had abated from the surface of the ground.
segments.literal: and-sent [object-marker]-the-dove from-with-him to-see have-lightened the-waters from-upon face-of the-ground

tokens.note: מֵאִתּוֹ: 'from with him', from his presence
הֲ introduces an indirect question; qalu from קלל, 'be light, slight'

phrases.english: Then he sent out the dove
to see whether the waters had abated
phrases.literal: 'to-see have-lightened the-waters'; קלל Qal, 'be slight, diminish'

phrases.english: from the surface of the ground

grammar: לִרְאוֹת הֲקַלּוּ: purpose clause (ל + infinitive) containing an indirect question introduced by the interrogative הֲ.
הֲקַלּוּ is a Qal perfect of the geminate root קלל, 'be light', here of waters 'lessening'.
The pashta on לִרְאוֹת and the zaqef qaton on הַמַּיִם mark off the content of the seeing.
הָאֲדָמָה, 'the ground', replaces הָאָרֶץ of verse 7; the dove is concerned with soil, not land at large.
segments.note: 'abated' keeps the sense of lightening (lessening of weight and amount). Rashi's reading of וַיְשַׁלַּח as release to go its own way is adopted in 'from him'.

commentary.summary: Rashi: the dove was sent at the end of seven days, since verse 10 says 'he waited another seven days', implying a first seven. This is an inference about dates and does not change the English.
Rashi: וַיְשַׁלַּח here is release (שִׁלּוּחַ), not a mission: she was let go to her own way, and if she found rest she would not return to him.
Onkelos: 'and he sent the dove from with him to see whether the waters had lightened (הֲקַלִּיאוּ)'.
Sforno: if the waters had lightened, the dove would nest in the mountains and towers as is her custom.

segments.english: But the dove found no resting place for the sole of her foot, and she returned to him in the ark, for there was water over the surface of all the earth. So he stretched out his hand, took her, and brought her to him into the ark.
segments.literal: and-not found the-dove resting-place for-sole-of her-foot and-returned to-him to the-ark for waters upon face-of all-the-earth and-sent his-hand and-took-her and-brought [obj]-her to-him to the-ark

tokens.note: מָנוֹחַ: place of rest; root נוח
כַּף־רֶגֶל: 'palm of the foot', the sole

phrases.english: But the dove found no resting place for the sole of her foot
and she returned to him in the ark
for there was water over the surface of all the earth
So he stretched out his hand

grammar: מַיִם עַל־פְּנֵי כָל־הָאָרֶץ gives the reason with כִּי; the clause has no verb (a nominal clause).
וַיִּשְׁלַח יָדוֹ, 'he sent his hand', is the idiom for reaching out; the same verb שׁלח is used of the birds in 8:7-8.
וַיִּקָּחֶהָ and אֹתָהּ carry the feminine object suffix: the dove is grammatically feminine.
The zaqef qaton after הַתֵּבָה divides the dove's failed search from the clause giving the reason.
segments.note: 'found no resting place' is the plain sense of מָנוֹחַ. The pronoun 'her' follows the Hebrew feminine; Rashi at 8:11 holds the dove was male.

commentary.summary: Ramban: birds do not rest on high bare mountain peaks, so the dove found no good resting place; the water still covered the earth's low ground.
Sforno: even the visible mountaintops were still very damp, so that even there she could not rest.

segments.english: He waited another seven days, and again he sent out the dove from the ark.
segments.literal: and-waited again seven-of days other and-added to-send [object-marker] the-dove from the-ark

tokens.note: wayyiqtol; the pack's lemma is חוּל, piel, and the lexicon entry has no 'piel wait' sense; I give the nearest listed sense. Rashi and Radak read it as 'waited' (cf. Job 29:21; Judges 3:25)
וַיֹּסֶף + infinitive: 'he added to do', i.e. 'he did again'

phrases.english: and again he sent out the dove

grammar: וַיֹּסֶף שַׁלַּח: a verb of adding with an infinitive means doing something again; 'he added to send' is 'he sent again'.
וַיָּחֶל is a rare form: Rashi takes it as 'waited' (לשון המתנה); Ibn Ezra says if it came from תוחלת it should be וַיְיַחֵל, and allows that it is an irregular word.
שִׁבְעַת יָמִים אֲחֵרִים: the number is in construct before the plural noun; אֲחֵרִים 'other' means a second week.
segments.note: The English 'waited' follows Rashi and the context. The lexicon sense is the nearest the entry offers and may belong rather to יָחַל; that is a limit of the data.

commentary.summary: Rashi: וַיָּחֶל is a term of waiting, like 'to me they listened and waited (וְיִחֵלּוּ)' (Job 29:21); there are many such in Scripture.
Ibn Ezra: in his view the word is not from תוחלת, for that would be וַיְיַחֵל; it may be an unusual word in grammar. The English takes the sense 'waited' regardless.
Ibn Ezra dates the sending to the twenty-fourth of Shevat; a calendar remark that does not bear on the English.
Radak: the root is חו״ל in the Hiphil, like 'they waited until they were ashamed' (Judges 3:25).
Onkelos: 'he waited (וְאוֹרִיךְ) another seven days and again sent the dove from the ark'.

segments.english: The dove came to him at evening time, and there in her beak was a freshly plucked olive leaf. So Noah knew that the waters had abated from the earth.
segments.literal: and-came to-him the-dove at-time-of evening and-behold leaf-of olive plucked in-her-mouth and-knew Noah that lightened the-waters from-upon the-earth

tokens.note: הִנֵּה draws attention to what Noah sees
טָרָף: see grammar notes; adjective or noun
בְּפִיהָ: 'in her mouth', a bird's beak

phrases.english: and there in her beak was a freshly plucked olive leaf

grammar: וְהִנֵּה turns the narration to what is seen at that moment: 'and there'.

טָרָף is the hard word. The qamets under the resh shows it is an adjective or noun, 'plucked' (Radak: a passive adjective, like טָרוּף); Ibn Ezra lists views: a doubled word like עֲלֵה/טָרָף, a superfluous ב, or an adjective.
The dove is feminine (בְּפִיהָ), but Rashi thinks the bird was male.
וַיֵּדַע נֹחַ כִּי־קַלּוּ: the verb of knowing takes a כִּי clause; קַלּוּ echoes הֲקַלּוּ of 8:8.
segments.note: 'freshly plucked' follows Radak and the BDB gloss; Rashi's 'snatched' (חָטַף) is close in sense. Beak is the bird's mouth. The feminine pronoun is kept.

commentary.summary: Rashi thinks the dove was male, since the text uses both genders; but every dove in Scripture is grammatically feminine (Song 5:12, Ezek 7:16, Hos 7:11). The English keeps 'her'.

Rashi: טָרָף means 'snatched' (חָטַף); the Aggadah takes it as 'food' and בְּפִיהָ as 'speech', the dove saying that she would rather have bitter food from God than sweet from flesh and blood. The homily is not adopted.

Ibn Ezra: some take טָרָף as a doubled word with the same sense as עֲלֵה; he prefers that the ב is extra, or that טָרָף is an adjective like חָכָם with passive sense like טָרוּף. So 'a plucked olive leaf'.
Ramban infers from the plain text that the trees were not uprooted or destroyed in the Flood; the Midrash holds that the leaf came from elsewhere. This bears on the setting, not on the words.
Radak: טָרָף is an adjective in place of a passive, like טָרוּף: the dove tore it from the olive tree; Noah saw that it was torn, not found floating.
Radak: קַלּוּ means 'diminished', for a small thing is light and a large one heavy.
Onkelos: 'a plucked (תְּבִיר) olive leaf in her mouth'.

segments.english: He waited another seven days and sent out the dove, and she did not return to him any more.
segments.literal: and-waited again seven-of days other and-sent [object-marker] the-dove and-not added to-return to-him again

tokens.note: יָסְפָה + infinitive: 'she added to', i.e. did again
עוֹד: 'again, still, any more'; Ibn Ezra takes it as 'ever'

phrases.english: and she did not return to him any more

grammar: וַיִּיָּחֶל is Niphal (not Hithpael, which would have a patah under the yod); the root is יחל, 'wait'.
לֹא־יָסְפָה שׁוּב: 'she did not add to return', the same idiom of repetition as in 8:10, now negative.
The disjunctive accents divide the verse into three: the waiting, the sending, the result.
The two forms וַיָּחֶל (8:10) and וַיִּיָּחֶל (8:12) differ in stem but say the same.
segments.note: The dove's failure to return is not explained in the text; Radak reads it as the dove finding rest.

commentary.summary: Rashi: this is the same as וַיָּחֶל but in a reflexive stem: the first is 'he waited', the second 'he was patient'.
Ibn Ezra: a Niphal form, as in וַיִּלָּחֶם and וַיִּצָּמֶד; the root is complete with the yod.
Ibn Ezra: עוֹד means 'forever', as in 'his uncleanness is still on him' and 'all the days of the earth'. The English 'any more' is close to this.
Radak: the form is Niphal from יח״ל; had it been Hithpael, the yod would be open (pataḥ), and it is qamets.
Radak: Noah knew then that the ground was dry and the dove had found rest on the earth and in many trees, so she did not come back.
Onkelos: 'and she did not again return to him any more'.

segments.english: In the six hundred and first year, in the first month, on the first of the month, the waters dried up from the earth. Noah removed the covering of the ark and looked, and there the surface of the ground had dried up.
segments.literal: and-it-was in-one and-six hundreds year in-the-first on-one of-the-month dried-up the-waters from-upon the-earth and-removed Noah [object-marker] covering-of the-ark and-saw and-behold dried-up face-of the-ground

tokens.note: wayyiqtol of היה as narrative formula
בְּאַחַת: 'in the one' of the six hundred
מֵאוֹת: plural of מֵאָה; the lexicon entry lists only 'hundredth', which does not fit, so I give no sense
qatal, 3rd plural; 'dried' of the water drained from the surface

phrases.literal: וַיְהִי is a narrative formula that introduces the date; there is no separate English word

phrases.english: In the six hundred and first year, in the first month
on the first of the month
the waters dried up from the earth
Noah removed the covering of the ark
and there the surface of the ground had dried up

grammar: The date is given in Hebrew order: year, month, day. 'the first' (הָרִאשׁוֹן) is the first month; the day is 'one' (אֶחָד).
חָרְבוּ הַמַּיִם and חָרְבוּ פְּנֵי הָאֲדָמָה: the verb חרב (dry up) is used of the waters and then of the surface of the ground; in 8:14 the verb is the stronger יבשׁ.
וַיַּרְא וְהִנֵּה: 'he saw, and behold': a narrative view of what Noah saw when the cover was open.
The telisha accents on וַיְהִי mark the start of a new section.
segments.note: The first month is Tishrei or Nisan (Rashi: R. Eliezer or R. Joshua). The text says only 'first'. The English keeps חרב as 'dried up' and יבשׁ in 8:14 as 'dry', following Rashi and Ibn Ezra on the difference.

commentary.summary: Rashi: 'the first month' is Tishrei according to R. Eliezer and Nisan according to R. Joshua (Rosh Hashanah 11b). The English says only 'the first month'.
Rashi: חָרְבוּ means it became like mud, for a crust formed on the upper surface. This is why 'dried up' here is not yet fully dry.
Ibn Ezra dates the dove's last sending to the first of Adar; the comment is about chronology and does not bear on the English.
Ibn Ezra: the ground was still soft, so a foot could not tread on it; only its surface had dried. Full dryness comes in verse 14.
Radak counts the year from Tishrei and gives dates; it concerns the calendar.
Sforno: Noah thought the surplus moisture in the air had dried; a remark on his reasoning.
Onkelos: 'in the six hundred and first year, in the first, on the first of the month the waters dried (נְגוּבוּ) from the earth'.

segments.english: In the second month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month, the earth was dry.
segments.literal: and-in-the-month the-second on-seven and-twenty day of-the-month was-dry the-earth

phrases.english: on the twenty-seventh day of the month

grammar: The date: month (the second), day (seven and twenty) of the month.
יָבְשָׁה הָאָרֶץ: the verb comes first and the subject, 'the earth', follows; the stem is Qal of יבשׁ.
The etnaḥta falls on לַחֹדֶשׁ, setting the date apart from the main clause.
The paragraph mark ס closes the section of the Flood's end.
segments.note: The verse uses יבשׁ, 'be dry', and not חרב as in 8:13; the English contrasts 'had dried up' with 'was dry' following Rashi's 'completely dry' (גָּרִיד כְּהִלְכָתָהּ).

commentary.summary: Rashi: the earth dried on the twenty-seventh of the second month; the eleven days are the excess of the solar year over the lunar, because the judgment of the generation of the Flood was a full year.
Rashi: יָבְשָׁה means it became fully dry as it should be (גָּרִיד כְּהִלְכָתָהּ).
Radak: the second month is Marheshvan; the rabbis say the days are the ten extra of the solar year. A calendar note.
Onkelos: 'in the second month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month, the earth was dry (יַבִּישַׁת)'.
